articles.title: How the media sold the Iraq War – and it’s doing it again on Iran
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content_excerpt: Iraq had “WMDs.” Now Iran has a “dirty bomb.” As CNN amplifies anonymous claims that Iran is plotting an attack on DC, BT Live’s Zoe Alexandra rewinds the tape on the corporate media blitz that sold us the Iraq War – from Colin Powell’s 2003 UN presentation on Saddam Hussein to the mainstream reporting that turned fake intelligence into an invasion. The playbook’s the same, and so is the goal: making a deeply unpopular war look necessary. Now Trump’s warning Iran is “looking at gases, looking at bio,” even as CNN’s own reporter admits the intel doesn’t indicate an imminent attack, and the White House concedes it knows of no credible threat. articles.title: China’s massive elections and politics beyond the ballot box
articles.author: Tings Chak
articles.content_excerpt: Lee en español aquí Across China, one of the world’s largest direct voting processes is underway. Throughout 2026 and 2027, more than one billion eligible voters are being called upon to elect over 2.6 million delegates to county and municipal people’s congresses. From the capital, Beijing, to the vast rural areas, the elections are being held on a scale rarely seen elsewhere; yet this facet of the Chinese political system remains little known abroad. articles.title: Garment workers in Bangladesh resume protests for better minimum wages
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content_excerpt: Security forces fired tear gas and stun grenades at thousands of workers protesting for better wages in Bangladesh’s capital, Dhaka, on the second consecutive day on Wednesday, November 18. The protesters, mostly women, marched across the city and blocked several roads, including the Dhaka-Meymensingh highway in and around the city and clashed with security forces setting their vehicles on fire at some places. Several workers were reportedly injured after the security forces’ crackdown. The security forces have also arrested scores of union leaders and agitating workers in the last two days accusing them of inciting violence. articles.title: Blue waves
articles.author: Sirantos Fotopoulos
articles.content_excerpt: M illions of Americans delivered a well-deserved rebuke to Trump on Election Day, but the Democratic Party would be wise to resist the temptation to mistake an electorate’s hatred of Republican authoritarianism for an endorsement of corporate liberalism. articles.title: “Defend the Sacred”: Indigenous Activist on Climate & Alaska Native Mary Peltola’s Senate Victory
articles.content_excerpt: Democrat Mary Peltola was declared the winner this week of Alaska’s closely watched race for U.S. Senate, making her the first Alaska Native lawmaker elected to the upper chamber of Congress. At the COP31 climate conference in Turkey, we speak with Aakaluk Adrienne Blatchford, an Inupiaq and Yup’ik organizer from Unalakleet, Alaska. She says Peltola’s win is a significant milestone for Indigenous peoples in Alaska. “Having somebody represent us in such a large capacity with such a big weight on her shoulders, but still carrying that struggle with her as she continues to advocate for our people and our way of life, is monumental,” says Blatchford.

articles.title: Russian Indigenous Activist Daria Egereva Remains Jailed; Arrested After 2025 U.N. Climate Talks
articles.content_excerpt: Human rights and climate groups are calling on Russia to release two prominent activists, Daria Egereva and Natalia Leongardt, who have been held in pretrial detention in Moscow for nearly a year, since December 2025. Egereva, a leading Indigenous rights activist in Russia, was arrested shortly after attending the COP30 United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil, where she served as co-chair of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change. Leongardt has worked for decades to support Indigenous rights. “Right now all we are demanding is the release of Daria and Natalia, because they shouldn’t be in prison. You shouldn’t be arrested for activism,” says Viktor Suliandziga-Bagat, an Indigenous rights activist and representative of the Udege people from the Russian Far East.

articles.title: Healthcare workers respond to a broken system by unionizing
articles.author: Dennis Kosuth
articles.content_excerpt: C hicago is seeing a burst of unionization amongst registered nurses – and it has become infectious, in the best sense of that word. In May of 2026, 77 percent of nurses at Rush University Medical Center (RUMC) voted in favor of joining the National Nurses Organizing Committee (NNOC). The 1,700 nurses at RUMC are now part of National Nurses United (NNU), a union that represents 225,000 nurses in healthcare settings across the United States. NNU was founded by a merger of nursing unions in 2009 and, in the past 17 years,has grown considerably from its initial strength of 150,000. The latest victory for NNOC took place in the first week of November when nurses who work for Endeavor Health at Edward Hospital in suburban Naperville, voted by a margin of 65 percent in favor of joining the union
